To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
flow-induced vasoreactivity in mesenteric arterial vessels is enhanced by endothelium-dependent factors, such as NO, endothelim-derived hyperpolarization, and ET- 1.
the vasoreactivity of the isolated rat mesenteric vascular beds to flow-induced shear stress is regulated by endothelially derived factors.
the flow rate-mediated increase of perfusion pressure is enhanced by N(G) -nitro-L -arginine plus methylene blue and slightly enhanced by tetraethylammonoium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the endothelium in the regulation of vascular tone in response to flow-induced shear stress.
the effects of shear stress on vascular tone.

the effects of endothelium-derived vasoactive agents (especially nitric oxide, endothelium-dependent hyperpolarizing factors and endothelin-1) on the flow-mediated vasodilator responses in rat mesenterial arterial beds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the response of vascular smooth muscle to flow stimulation is not simply mediated by NO and/or EDHF, but is subtly regulated by a variety of endothelium-derived substances.
the flow-induced vasorelaxation is mediated via NO, EDHF, and ET- 1.
flow-induced shear stress stimulates the endothelial cells, resulting in the release of NO, EDRF, and ET- 1, which, in turn, modulate the vascular tone of mesenteric arterial vessels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NO, EDHF, and ET- 1 are all involved in the flow rate-induced vasodilation in the mesenteric arterial vasculature.
the response of vascular resistance to flow stimulation is regulated in a complex manner, involving endothelium-dependent factors and the interaction between them.
the endothelium-derived NO and endothelium-derived vasoconstrictor factors are the major mediators of flow-induced vasoreactivity in the rat mesenteric vascular bed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
flow-induced shear stress may play a role in the regulation of vascular function in the mesenteric bed.
the flow-induced increase in perfusate nitrite level and ET-1 content is associated with a flow-dependent increase in mesenteric vascular tone.

flow-induced vasoreactivity in mesenteric arterial vasculature is dependent on endothelium-derived vasorelaxant factors, and that these factors play a significant role in the regulation of the response of vascular resistance to changes in flow.
